cues.text: Chapter four: Distributed transactions.
Let's start with the core problem.
Sometimes a single transaction has to cross more than one site.
When that happens, we need two things.
First, atomic agreement: every site must reach the same outcome, either all of them commit or all of them abort.
Second, isolation: the transaction must still be kept properly separated from other concurrent transactions, even though its work is spread across locations.
The classic mechanism for atomic agreement is two-phase commit, usually shortened to 2PC.
As the name suggests, it has two phases.
The first is the prepare phase.
Here, each participant votes on whether it is able to commit.
The second is the decision phase, where a coordinator orders either a commit or an abort.
The rule is simple: if any participant votes no, the decision is abort.
There is a well-known weakness, though.
A participant that has prepared may block if the coordinator fails and the decision is not available to it.
It has promised it can commit, so it cannot safely decide on its own, and it has to wait.
One more point to keep clear: 2PC coordinates atomic commit.
It is not consensus by itself.
Those are not the same thing.
Now an example.
Suppose we debit a Kano account and credit an Enugu account.
Both sites prepare.
Only if both are ready does the coordinator commit.
And here is the rule to remember: never credit alone after an uncertain debit.
If you are not sure the debit succeeded, you must not go ahead and credit the other account by itself.
Atomic commit is only half the story, because we also need concurrency control.
Distributed locks and timestamp ordering can both be used to enforce it.
But there are costs.
Cross-region round trips increase latency, so every coordination step that has to travel between regions makes things slower.
And deadlock detection is harder across nodes, because the waiting relationships are spread over several machines rather than sitting in one place.
Finally, there is a different approach for long workflows: the saga.
A saga breaks a long workflow into a series of local transactions, each paired with a compensating action.
Take an order.
The system reserves inventory, requests payment, and confirms delivery.
If something fails along the way, it releases the reservations and refunds the customer if appropriate.
Notice an important point here.
Compensation is a business action, not an exact rollback.
You are not magically erasing what happened; you are performing a new action that makes up for it.
Sagas also depend on reliable messaging.
Idempotent message handling, meaning that processing the same message twice has the same effect as processing it once, together with a transactional outbox, reduces duplicate or lost effects.
